notable_claims: Extracurricular activities can be prohibited without violating academic freedom if conditions of scarcity, purpose, consistency, fairness, and availability of alternatives are met.
Resource quotas (CPU and disk space) may resolve conflicts between educational needs and free expression.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie proposes a set of criteria to determine when prohibiting extracurricular activity on university computers is compatible with academic freedom. He argues that such prohibitions are only legitimate if resources are scarce, the machine is dedicated to specific classes, enforcement is consistent and fair, and alternative machines exist for free expression.
classification.title: Free Forum vs. Class-Work Only machines

identity.subject: Free Forum vs. Class-Work Only machines

notable_claims: Free expression on computers is analogous to extracurricular expression in classrooms.
Administrative 'say-so' should not be sufficient to prohibit free expression on university machines if resources are abundant.
The default mode for universities should be to allow, protect, and promote free expression.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie argues against restricting university computer use to strictly academic purposes, contrasting 'free expression' with other types of unauthorized activity like chemistry experiments. He contends that because free expression is central to academic freedom and protected by the First Amendment, computers should be treated as campus facilities for expression unless resources are critically limited. He suggests that administrative mandates alone are insufficient to override the default university mission of promoting free inquiry.
classification.title: Re: Free Forum vs. Class-Work Only machines

identity.subject: Re: Free Forum vs. Class-Work Only machines

notable_claims: Password sharing undermines the ability to pin down problems and hold users accountable for system damage.
Encryption is a viable solution for users concerned about system administrators reading private files.
classification.summary: Pete Hartman responds to questions regarding system security and user privacy. He argues that prohibiting password sharing is necessary for accountability when tracking system damage. He suggests that users who fear administrator access to private files may simply be too lazy to use encryption.
classification.title: Re: System Maintenance/Security requirements

notable_claims: Students at private colleges have contractual rather than constitutional rights.
Campus handbooks and registration agreements create legally enforceable obligations regarding due process, expression, and privacy.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie responds to a student's inquiry regarding the legal protections available at private colleges compared to public ones. He explains that while constitutional rights may not apply, students have enforceable contractual rights defined in campus handbooks and policy documents. He argues that computer policies contradicting these contractual obligations are legally and morally indefensible.
classification.title: Public/Private institutions

notable_claims: University lawyers may approve vague policies without understanding how system administrators will actually interpret and enforce them.
The NCSA's prohibition of email that 'attempts to disadvantage NCSA' was interpreted by its security officer to prohibit strong criticisms of the organization.
Ohio State University's ACS policy lacked explicit due process protections, such as notice of rights or appeal mechanisms for denied access.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie argues that university lawyers are often unqualified to review computer policies due to a lack of technical understanding and the vagueness of policy language. He provides examples from the University of Illinois (NCSA) and Ohio State University where vague terms allowed for interpretations that potentially violated the First Amendment and academic freedom. Kadie advocates for explicit policies created with faculty and student participation.
classification.title: Authority of Public Universities

notable_claims: ALA policies suggest that no challenged material should be removed based on the request of a single person without committee review or administrative concurrence.
organizations: Michigan Association for Media in Education
classification.summary: Carl Kadie recommends several manuals on library science and intellectual freedom to illustrate how librarians handle censorship attempts. He highlights the American Library Association's policies regarding material selection and the requirement for committee review before removing challenged items. The note suggests these traditional library frameworks may be applicable to newsgroups.
classification.title: Censorship and Selection

notable_claims: Case studies from Ohio State and other universities highlight a lack of due process in computer-related expulsions.
The Berkeley Open Computing Facility (OCF) is cited as a model for democratic management of computer resources.
Debates occurred regarding whether the possession of nude GIF images constitutes sexual harassment or violates student rights.
Proposed U.S. constitutional amendments were discussed to explicitly guarantee civil liberties on computers and networks.
classification.summary: A collection of abstracts for the first twenty issues of the Computers and Academic Freedom News (CAF-news). The digests document early debates on netnews censorship, user privacy, due process in computer policy enforcement, and the democratic management of resources.
classification.title: CAF-News Abstracts

notable_claims: System administrators at Case Western and Purdue censored outgoing newsgroup messages.
User/sysadmin conflict is often attributed to differing perceptions of computer systems.
Denial of due process for users can lead them to take matters into their own hands, causing more serious problems.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie provides corrections to the 'eff.org:academic/abstracts' file via a diff. The updates clarify details regarding Netnews censorship at Purdue and Case Western Reserve University, as well as reports of system administrator abuse at the University of Kentucky. Kadie also issues an apology to Wes Morgan for using hyperbolic language regarding user-driven pressure on sysadmins.
classification.title: Re: CAF-News Abstracts
